docs.text: Mol-JEPA Embedding Pipeline Authors: James Bannon , Michael Tran, Matthew Boccalon Contact: bhklab.jamesbannon@gmail.com Description: Pipeline for Generating Mol-JEPA Embeddings from HDD Compounds This pipeline produces embeddings based on the pre-trained Mol-JEPA architecture . The pipeline functions by downloading data from the Harmonized Drug Dataset ( HDD v3 ), selecting a compound universe of compounds with at least some labeled data, and using the pre-trained Mol-JEPA Architecture to produce the embeddings based on the compound's SMILES string. At present the embeddings are the <CLS> token generated by the Mol-JEPA model. Concretely, for constructing the drug universe we only keep molecules which are either: - In the Tox21 dataset Or have non-missing entry for at least one of the following columns in the HDD file coldata.tsv : "ATC.Code", "Mechanism.of.Action", "FDA.Approved", 'BBB.Permeable', "LTKB.DILI.Annotation" , "DILIrank.DILI.Severity.Grade", "DILIrank.DILI.Annotation", "DILIst.DILI.Annotation", "Livertox.Hepatotoxicity.Likelihood.Score", "Livertox.Hepatotoxicity.Likelihood.Reason", "DIRIL.Label.Gong", "DIRIL.Label.Shi", "DIRIL.Toxicity", "DICT.Cardiotoxicity", "DICT.Label.Section", "LTKB.DILI.Severity.Grade", "DICT.Concern", "DICT.Keywords"` The code here can be run locally and also as a Nextflow pipeline. At present the embeddings are the <CLS> token generated by the Mol-JEPA model. Running Locally Pixi is required to run this project. If you haven't installed it yet, follow these instructions . Once you've done follow these steps: Clone this repository to your local machine Navigate to the project directory Set up the environment using Pixi: pixi install Next navigate to workflow/scripts and run the folowing commands in order: pixi run "python3 download.py" pixi run "python3 construct_drug_universe.py" pixi run "python3 generate_embeddings.py" This will put the resulting embeddings in the data/results folder. Running with Nextflow Install Pixi . The locked environment includes Nextflow and Java. From the repository root: bash pixi install --locked pixi run --locked pipeline Nextflow downloads colData.tsv and Tox21.tsv using config/downloads.yaml , builds the molecule universe, and generates embeddings. The first run also downloads the pretrained Mol-JEPA model. The default device in config/embeddings.yaml is CPU. 3. Find molecule_embeddings.csv , embedding_qc.html , and the Nextflow trace, report, and timeline in data/results/nextflow/ . When the workflow builds the universe, it also writes data/results/nextflow/data/procdata/molecule_universe.txt . Keep data/work/ and .nextflow/ to resume a run: bash pixi run --locked pipeline -- -resume To reuse local HDD inputs, pass the directory that contains HDD/colData.tsv and HDD/Tox21.tsv : pixi run --locked pipeline -- --raw_data data/rawdata --outdir data/results/nextflow Compounds missing SMILES or a PubChem CID are skipped. Join the output back to the universe on HDD.Compound.ID to check coverage. Add --molset path/to/molecule_universe.txt to reuse a list of HDD compound IDs (one per line). Use --downloads or --embeddings to pass an alternate YAML config. Run pixi run --locked pipeline -- --help to see the workflow options. To regenerate the QC HTML without recomputing embeddings: pixi run --locked qc This reads the default Nextflow CSV and local data/rawdata/HDD/colData.tsv . If Nextflow downloaded into its work cache, pass that run's exact labels TSV: pixi run --locked qc path/to/molecule_embeddings.csv path/to/HDD/colData.tsv path/to/output For applet builds and container uploads, see Deploying on DNAnexus .

Proper documentation ensures reproducibility and helps others understand your research methodology. How to Document Your Data For each data source, include the following information: 1. External Data Sources Name : Official name of the dataset Version/Date : Version number or access date URL : Link to the data source Access Method : How the data was obtained (direct download, API, etc.) Access Date : When the data was accessed/retrieved Data Format : Format of the data (FASTQ, DICOM, CSV, etc.) Citation : Proper academic citation if applicable License : Usage restrictions and attribution requirements Example: ## TCGA RNA-Seq Data - **Name**: The Cancer Genome Atlas RNA-Seq Data - **Version**: Data release 28.0 - March 2021 - **URL**: https://portal.gdc.cancer.gov/ - **Access Method**: GDC Data Transfer Tool - **Access Date**: 2021-03-15 - **Citation**: The Cancer Genome Atlas Network. (2012). Comprehensive molecular portraits of human breast tumours. Nature, 490(7418), 61-70. - **License**: [NIH Genomic Data Sharing Policy](https://sharing.nih.gov/genomic-data-sharing-policy) 2. Internal/Generated Data Name : Descriptive name of the dataset Creation Date : When the data was generated Creation Method : Brief description of how the data was created Input Data : What source data was used Processing Scripts : References to scripts/Github Repo used to generate this data Example: ## Processed RNA-Seq Data - **Name**: Processed RNA-Seq Data for TCGA-BRCA - **Creation Date**: 2021-04-01 - **Creation Method**: Processed using kallisto and DESeq2 - **Input Data**: FASTQ Data obtained from the SRA database - **Processing Scripts**: [GitHub Repo](https://github.com/tcga-brca-rnaseq) 3. Data Dictionary For complex datasets, include a data dictionary that explains: Column Name Data Type Description Units Possible Values patient_id string Unique patient identifier N/A TCGA-XX-XXXX format age integer Patient age at diagnosis years 18-100 expression float Gene expression value TPM Any positive value Best Practices Store raw data in data/rawdata/ and never modify it Store processed data in data/procdata/ and all code used to generate it should be in workflow/scripts/ Document all processing steps Track data provenance (where data came from and how it was modified) Respect data usage agreements and licenses! This is especially important for data that should not be shared publicly

docs.text: Developer Notes Purpose of This Section This section is for documenting technical decisions, challenges, and solutions encountered during your project. These notes are valuable for: Future you (who will forget why certain decisions were made) Collaborators who join the project later People coming from your publication who want to reproduce your work Anyone who might want to extend your research What to Document Design Decisions Document important decisions about your project's architecture, algorithms, or methodologies: ## Choice of RNA-Seq Analysis Pipeline [2025-04-25] We chose the kallisto over STAR pipeline for the following reasons: 1. The CCLE dataset is very large, and kallisto is faster for quantifying large datasets 2. GDSC used kallisto, so we can compare our results with theirs Technical Challenges Record significant problems you encountered and how you solved them ## Sample Name Format Issue [2025-04-25] We encountered a problem with sample name formats between the CCLE and GDSC datasets. The CCLE dataset uses "BRCA-XX-XXXX" format, while the GDSC dataset uses "BRCA-XX-XXXX-XX". We had to write a script to remove the last two characters from the sample names in the GDSC dataset. Dependencies and Environment Document specific version requirements or compatibility issues: ## Critical Version Dependencies [2025-04-25] SimpleITK 2.4.1 introduced a bug that flips images, so we froze version 2.4.0 Best Practices Date your entries when appropriate Link to relevant code files or external resources Include small code snippets when helpful Note alternatives you considered and why they were rejected Document failed approaches to prevent others from repeating mistakes Update notes when major changes are made to the approach

docs.text: Deploying on DNAnexus The Docker image contains the locked Linux Pixi environment. The applet contains the Nextflow workflow, config, Python scripts, and QC notebook. Build and upload them separately. Build a Linux AMD64 image and export it in Docker archive format: bash mkdir -p data/dnanexus docker build --platform linux/amd64 -t mol-jepa:v1 . docker save -o data/dnanexus/mol-jepa-v1.tar mol-jepa:v1 The current Linux lockfile is CPU-only. The image does not contain the HDD inputs or Mol-JEPA weights. By default the job downloads the HDD files from Zenodo and the model from Hugging Face, which requires outbound network access. Upload the archive to a DNAnexus project that can build and run Nextflow applets. Record the returned file ID: bash dx login dx mkdir -p 'project-PROJECT_ID:/containers' dx mkdir -p 'project-PROJECT_ID:/applets' dx upload data/dnanexus/mol-jepa-v1.tar \ --path 'project-PROJECT_ID:/containers/' --brief Package the source and build the applet. Replace source.XXXXXX with the directory printed by the packaging script: bash bash workflow/scripts/package_dnanexus.sh dx build --nextflow data/dnanexus/source.XXXXXX \ --profile dnanexus --nextflow-version 25.10 \ --extra-args '{"name":"mol-jepa-embedding-pipeline","title":"Mol-JEPA Embedding Pipeline","summary":"Generate Mol-JEPA embeddings for HDD compounds."}' \ --destination 'project-PROJECT_ID:/applets/mol-jepa-embedding-pipeline' Run the applet and pass the image file URI. Use a relative outdir . For a first test, upload a small list of eligible HDD IDs (with SMILES and PubChem CID) and pass it as molset : bash dx run applet-APPLET_ID \ -icontainer_image='dx://project-PROJECT_ID:file-IMAGE_ID' \ -imolset='project-PROJECT_ID:file-MOLSET_ID' \ -ioutdir=results --destination 'project-PROJECT_ID:/' Check that molecule_embeddings.csv has exactly the test IDs once each and 512 finite values per ID. Open or download the embedding_qc.html output. Small runs omit panels without enough matched labels. Omit molset for the full universe. See the DNAnexus Nextflow guide for platform setup and Docker image options.
